rem:groebner-nf-computation:
Remark Gröbner--Shirshov normal form computation with quotient ideals. The Gröbner--Shirshov normal form \mathcal{N}(Z, N) of a nucleus in H_A(q) is a formal sum over reduced braid words:

  \mathcal{N}(Z, N)
  = 
  \sum_{w \in \mathrm{supp}} c_w \cdot w.

Each amplitude c_w \in \mathbb{Z}[q^{1/2}, q^{-1/2}] is an exact Laurent polynomial in the aether parameter q. The support \mathrm{supp} \subset S_A consists of reduced words in the symmetric group.

Content of the NF

Each reduced word w of length \ell(w) represents a configuration of \ell(w) simultaneously active crossings in the nuclear braid. The amplitude of this configuration is c_w.

The word length \ell has a direct physical interpretation:

See Table 1.

The weight distribution W(\ell) = \sum_{|w| = \ell} |c_w| defines the total amplitude at each correlation level. For all computed nuclei with A \leq 12:

  • W(L_{\max}) \gg W(0). The fully correlated state carries the largest amplitude. This determines the shell binding energy via many-body correlations.
  • W(0) + W(1). This is the amplitude in the optimal basis \{\mathbf{1}, \sigma_0, \ldots, \sigma_{A-2}\}. The transfer matrix computes this directly via traced volumes \hat{V}_i.
  • W(\ell) / W(\ell - 1) \approx q^{c}. The weight grows exponentially. Each Hecke reduction \sigma_i^2 = (q - q^{-1})\sigma_i + 1 transfers amplitude from degree \ell to degrees \ell - 1 and \ell - 2. This scales by q - q^{-1} \approx 0.209.

Quotient ideals reduce A! to A

The raw normal form contains up to |S_A| = A! terms. For nuclei in the valley of stability with N \geq Z - 1, two quotient ideals reduce this to exactly A terms. This forms the optimal Gröbner--Shirshov basis.

I_8 (adjacency correlation). A reduced word \sigma_i \sigma_{i+1} of length 2 is absorbed into the single-generator term \sigma_{i+1} when the latter is present. The coefficient of \sigma_i \sigma_{i+1} matches the off-diagonal entry of the transfer matrix product M_i at \sigma_i.

Adjacency correlation represents the non-commutative coupling between neighbouring crossings. It appears as the off-diagonal entry of the 2 \times 2 transfer matrix T(c, d) acting on the Hecke state (a \sigma + b). The optimal basis encodes this coupling in the ratio c_{\sigma_i \sigma_{i+1}} / c_{\sigma_{i+1}}, which is a function of q alone.

I_9 (closed shell chain collapse). A reduced word w \cdot \sigma_j is absorbed when its prefix w is present. Apply this recursively from longest to shortest words. This collapses the entire normal form to the standard basis \{\mathbf{1}, \sigma_0, \ldots, \sigma_{A-2}\}.

Each generator \sigma_i contributes a transfer matrix chain M_i = \prod_{j > i} T_{K_i, K_j}(q). The extension w \cdot \sigma_j represents the next step in this chain. The chain collapses to a single term \hat{V}_i = z \cdot (M_i)_{00} + (M_i)_{10}. This yields the Markov-traced volume.

Necessity of d \neq 0 for I_9. Multiply the normal form by (c \cdot \sigma_k + d). This scales every existing word by d and extends each word by c \cdot \sigma_k. For every extended word w \cdot \sigma_k, the prefix w survives from the d-term. This allows I_9 to absorb it. This mechanism fails if d = 0.

For proton–proton crossings, d = 0. Without the prefix, I_9 lacks an anchor for chain stripping. The condition d \neq 0 holds for neutron–neutron (d = -(q - q^{-1})) and proton–neutron (d = -(q - q^{-1})/2) crossings. The valley of stability condition N \geq Z - 1 ensures at least one d \neq 0 crossing at every generator.

The histogram is universal in A

The term-count histogram h(\ell) = \#\{w : |w| = \ell\} tallies reduced words at each length. This is verified for A \leq 8. The histogram is identical for all (Z, N) at the same A, such as {}^8\mathrm{Be}(4,4) and {}^8\mathrm{Li}(3,5).

The histogram depends only on the Iwahori--Hecke algebra H_A(q). It factors as a product of q-integers:

See Table 2.

These are q-multinomial coefficients. The palindromicity of the histogram polynomial reflects the Poincaré duality of the Bruhat order on the support. This is verified up to A \leq 7.

The weight distribution carries the pairing energy

The A-universal histogram depends only on A. The weight distribution W(\ell) depends on (Z, N). At constant A:

  • Even-even nuclei exhibit higher total weight. This reflects stronger coherence from nucleon pairing.
  • Odd-odd nuclei exhibit lower total weight. Unpaired crossings weaken the chain anchor.

The ratio \mathrm{net}(\text{even-even}) / \mathrm{net}(\text{odd-odd}) quantifies the pairing energy. At A = 6, \mathrm{net}({}^6\mathrm{He}(2,4)) / \mathrm{net}({}^6\mathrm{Li}(3,3)) = 6.64 / 4.96 = 1.34. This represents a 34\% pairing enhancement.

In the normal form, adjacent same-type crossings (even occupancy) trigger the Hecke product \sigma^2 = (q - q^{-1})\sigma + 1. The generated \mathbf{1} term anchors the I_9 chain. Unpaired crossings (odd occupancy) produce only the \sigma term. This weakens the anchor and reduces the total amplitude.

The Pauli factor is a multi-generator phenomenon

The alternating trace \mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{alt}} = \sum_w c_w \cdot (-q^{-1})^{\ell(w)} evaluates each word at the alternating eigenvalue -q^{-1}. The ratio

  F_{\mathrm{Pauli}}^{(A)}
  = 
  \frac{|\mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{alt}}(\mathcal{N})|}{|\mathrm{net}(\mathcal{N})|}

measures the normal form amplitude residing in the alternating irrep of S_A. This is the antisymmetric channel governed by Pauli exclusion.

This quantity eludes the 2 \times 2 transfer matrix. The per-generator transfer matrix has only eigenvalues q and -q^{-1}. Both the symmetric and alternating irreps share these. Irrep separation demands the multi-generator interaction, determining how \sigma_0 and \sigma_1 act together. This requires the full Gröbner--Shirshov normal form.

The 6 \times 6 transfer matrix provides no shortcut

An enlarged 6 \times 6 transfer matrix acting on the H_3(q) basis might appear sufficient to separate the irreducible representations.

Symbolic proof shows otherwise. The matrix T_6(c, d) = c \cdot R(\sigma_0) + d \cdot I_6 possesses exactly two distinct eigenvalues, each with multiplicity 3:

  \lambda_+ = c \cdot q + d,
  \qquad
  \lambda_- = c \cdot (-q^{-1}) + d.

These match the 2 \times 2 eigenvalues. The standard irrep contains both eigenvalues because \sigma_0 in the standard representation has a 2 \times 2 matrix with both eigenvalues. The 6 \times 6 matrix fails to separate the symmetric from the standard irrep, or the alternating from the standard irrep.

The Pauli factor F_{\mathrm{Pauli}} is irreducibly multi-generator. No per-generator transfer matrix can compute it.

The Pauli exclusion principle acts between pairs of fermions, not on individual crossings. Quarks inside a Borromean triplet embody this. The multi-generator structure encodes this inter-quark correlation.

Computed witnesses are exact in \mathbb{Z}[\check{q}, \check{q}^{-1}] for A \leq 12. They display at q_0:

The denominator 2^{p_n} is tracked separately.

The H_3(q) Pauli factor is F_{\mathrm{Pauli}} = 0.6382. The A-strand values differ because they capture the full multi-generator interaction, not the 3-strand projection.

Streaming pattern discovery

During inductive construction, the quotient ideals I_8 and I_9 strip terms at each strand boundary. The engine identifies the most frequent suffix patterns before stripping. This suggests candidates for new structural ideals.

rem:kummer-shell-closure:
Remark Shell closure as \mu_n torsion in the Kummer tower. The Kummer tower filtration provides the algebraic framework for shell closure, the Pauli factor, and the odd-odd pairing deficit in the Gröbner--Shirshov normal form.

The \mu_2 torsion as Pauli evaluation

The alternating trace of the normal form evaluates each word w at the alternating eigenvalue (-q^{-1})^{\ell(w)}:

  \mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{alt}}(\mathcal{N})
  = 
  \sum_{w \in \mathrm{supp}} c_w \cdot (-q^{-1})^{\ell(w)}

This sum is the \mu_2 Kummer evaluation. It applies the sign character of \mathbb{G}_m to the normal form. The eigenvalue -q^{-1} is the alternating root of the Hecke relation \sigma^2 = (q - q^{-1})\sigma + 1. The eigenvalue q is the symmetric root.

The Pauli factor measures the \mu_2-torsion content:

  F_{\mathrm{Pauli}}^{(A)}
  = 
  \frac{|\mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{alt}}(\mathcal{N})|}{|\mathrm{net}(\mathcal{N})|}

It quantifies the amplitude present in the antisymmetric channel.

Shell closure as Kummer divisibility

The Kummer reduction at level n takes the form:

  \kappa_0 \bmod n = 0

  n  \big|  \chi(A)

The obstruction vanishes when n divides the Euler characteristic \chi(A) of the brane configuration. Apply this to the nuclear braid.

rem:nf-computation-strategy:
Remark Computational strategy for the Gröbner--Shirshov normal form. The Gröbner--Shirshov normal form computation separates into three complexity regimes.

The three regimes

Regime 1: Transfer matrix (O(A^2)). The optimal normal form \{\mathbf{1}, \sigma_0, \ldots, \sigma_{A-2}\} possesses coefficients equal to the Markov-traced volumes \hat{V}_i(q). Each \hat{V}_i is a product of A - i - 1 transfer matrices T(c_j, d_j). This requires \binom{A}{2} multiplications. This yields the Q-value, the Skein polynomial, and the optimal normal form coefficients without Iwahori--Hecke algebra expansion.

Regime 2: Symbolic Gröbner--Shirshov with stripping (O(A^3)). The full normal form dictates the Pauli factor F_{\mathrm{Pauli}}, the color content, and the per-length weight distribution. Apply inductive quotient stripping with ideals I_{8} and I_{9} after each strand. This bounds the intermediate term count to O(A^2) per strand, yielding O(A^3) overall. All coefficients remain exact Laurent polynomials in \mathbb{Z}[t, t^{-1}].

Regime 3: Full expansion (O(A!)). Without stripping, the raw normal form generates up to A! terms. This limits tractability to A \leq 9. The full expansion exposes the raw histogram and palindromic structure. It contributes to no physical observable.

Inductive quotient chaining

Apply the chain collapse ideal I_{9} at each strand boundary. The Pauli data of stripped terms are accumulated as symbolic polynomials. The surviving optimal basis contains roughly A terms. The subsequent strand computation initiates from these A terms, bypassing the A! explosion.

The accumulation is exact. Each stripped term contributes its coefficient c_w(t) to the running totals \mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{alt}}(t) and \mathrm{net}(t). This is weighted by (-t^{-2})^{\ell(w)} for the alternating trace. The final witness sums the accumulated stripped and surviving contributions.

Only stripped terms are accumulated. If all terms were accumulated before stripping, surviving terms would double-count when contributing to subsequent strands.

The bottleneck: strand 8

For nuclei with A > 8, the computation exhibits a characteristic bottleneck:

  1. Strands 1–7: The normal form builds to \sim 14{,}000 terms at A = 8, or \sim 230{,}000 terms at A = 9. This takes under 10 seconds.
  2. Strand 8 boundary: The I_{9} strip collapses \sim 230{,}000 terms to roughly 9 terms. The Pauli data for the stripped terms are accumulated.
  3. Strands 9+: Each strand expands from \sim 10 terms to 5{,}000–240{,}000 terms. It then strips back to 10–600 terms at the boundary.

The bottleneck is the final crossing of a large strand. This typically involves neutron–neutron crossings characterized by c = 1, d = -(q - q^{-1}). Peak memory occurs immediately before stripping.

Optimisation strategies

Monomial ordering (LenLex). Use length-lexicographic ordering. The engine reduces shorter words first, then applies lexicographic ordering within the same degree. This aligns with the Iwahori--Hecke algebra. The Hecke relation \sigma_i^2 = (q - q^{-1})\sigma_i + 1 acts as the sole degree-changing rule.

Junction-only reduction. When appending \sigma_k to a reduced word w, only the junction is checked. The prefix w remains reduced. This lowers the amortized per-word reduction cost from O(\ell) to O(1).

Separated reduction pools. Terms are partitioned into stable fully-reduced and pending pools. Stable terms are never rescanned. When a pending term collides with a stable term, the merged result returns to the pending pool.

Batch quotient stripping (O(A \cdot L_{\max})). The I_{9} strip processes all terms at each length level simultaneously. It descends from longest to shortest words. All terms containing a specific length \ell - 1 prefix are collected and removed. This operates in O(n \cdot L_{\max}) rather than O(n^2).

Mid-crossing stripping. For large strands, the quotient strip fires within a crossing multiplication once the term count exceeds 30,000. This halts the exponential blowup from cascaded adjacent generators.

Pattern discovery. At each strand boundary, the engine identifies frequent suffix patterns. These candidate sub-words suggest structural ideals beyond I_{8} and I_{9}. Persisting patterns indicate universal structural operations eligible for inclusion in the quotient ideal.

rem:skein-shell-correction:
Remark Shell corrections from Skein polynomial factorization of the multi-nucleon link. The Skein binding Lagrangian (Skein binding Lagrangian) derives the smooth, liquid-drop nuclear binding energy directly from the categorical action. This derivation predicts that neutron excess grows with p. However, it misses the shell structure. Nuclei exhibit anomalously high binding at the stability pairs \{2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82, 126\}. Shell corrections demand a discrete term in the binding energy. This escapes the smooth continuous formula.

The gap in the derivation.

The chain from the R-matrix to nuclear binding proceeds as:

  \mathcal{R} \xrightarrow{\text{Yang--Baxter}}
  \check{R} \xrightarrow{\text{crossing asymmetry}}
  \mathfrak{E}_{\mathrm{cross}} \xrightarrow{\text{Skein binding}}
  \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{bind}} \xrightarrow{\partial/\partial p}
  p^*(A).

The final beta-stability step yields the smooth curve. The missing step is a discrete correction \delta E_{\mathrm{shell}}(p, n). This is nonzero only when the multi-nucleon link \mathcal{N}(Z, N) (stable nucleus) possesses a specific topological structure.

Conjecture: shell correction from closed sub-links.

Let \mathcal{N}(Z, N) = Z\mathfrak{p} \oplus N\mathfrak{n} be a multi-nucleon link. The Skein polynomial J_{\mathcal{N}}(q) factors into a product of Skein polynomials of closed sub-links at specific (p, n) values. The shell correction is:

  \delta E_{\mathrm{shell}}(p, n)
  = 
  -\lambda_{\mathrm{shell}} \cdot
  \sum_{\text{closed sub-links } L_i \subset \mathcal{N}}
  \frac{|J_{L_i}(q)|}{|J_{\mathcal{N}}(q)|}.

The sum runs over maximal closed unlinked sub-links L_i of \mathcal{N}. The shell energy scale is \lambda_{\mathrm{shell}}.

Closed sub-links of \mathcal{N}(Z, N).

A closed sub-link of \mathcal{N}(Z, N) is a subset S \subset \{1, \ldots, p+n\} of nucleons satisfying two conditions:

  1. The restriction \mathcal{N}|_S of the Hopf link to S forms a split link. It can be isotoped into a ball disjoint from all remaining nucleons.
  2. The Skein polynomial of \mathcal{N}|_S divides J_{\mathcal{N}}. Then J_{\mathcal{N}} = J_{\mathcal{N}|_S} \cdot J_{\mathcal{N}|_{S^c}} \cdot (\text{linking factor}).

When these hold, the link factorizes. The nucleons in S form an internally bound cluster. They contribute extra binding energy beyond the liquid-drop prediction.

Predicted factorizations.

For the Descartes universe (\chi = -6), the predicted factorizations are:

See Table.

The \alpha particle \mathcal{N}(2,2) acts as the fundamental closed sub-link. Its Skein polynomial factorizes completely. Stability pair nuclei are precisely those where the maximum possible number of \alpha clusters form. They saturate all available Hopf junctions.

The \alpha-cluster hypothesis.

The closed sub-link structure predicts the shell correction is largest when (p, n) admits the exact factorization:

  \mathcal{N}(Z, N) = 
  k \times \mathcal{N}(2, 2)  \oplus 
  (p - 2k)\mathfrak{p}  \oplus

where k = \min(\lfloor p/2 \rfloor, \lfloor n/2 \rfloor). The shell energy becomes:

  =

  = 
  -\lambda_{\mathrm{shell}} \cdot
  \min\!\left(\left\lfloor \frac{p}{2} \right\rfloor,
  \left\lfloor \frac{n}{2} \right\rfloor\right).

This quantity is maximised when both p and n are even. Even-even nuclei host the most \alpha clusters. It is locally maximised at the stability pairs, where the factorization is complete.

Remaining obligations.

  1. Skein factorization: It remains to prove that the Skein polynomial J_{\mathcal{N}(Z, N)}(q) factors when (p, n) admits an \alpha-cluster decomposition. This requires a direct computation in the Skein algebra of the Hopf link.
  2. Shell energy scale: It remains to derive \lambda_{\mathrm{shell}} directly from the categorical action. It is expected to be expressible in terms of q, a_V, and the Skein polynomial of \mathcal{N}(2,2).
  3. Corrected stability formula: It remains to show that the total binding energy \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{bind}} + \delta E_{\mathrm{shell}} reproduces all observed stable isotopes to within |\Delta n| \leq 1 for all p \leq 103.
  4. Genus lift: It remains to show that including \delta E_{\mathrm{shell}} lifts the stability cubic from genus 0 to genus 1.

prop:shell-structure-eigenvalues:
Proposition Orbital shells from eigenvalues of the photon-electron transfer matrix. Conditional on Quarks as Borromean-linked unknots in the exceptional divisor. The eigenvalues of the photon-electron transfer matrix T_{\gamma e}(q) determine the orbital shell structure of an atom. Shell n corresponds to the n-th power T_{\gamma e}^n. The shell energies satisfy a Chebyshev recurrence in q.

The characteristic polynomial

The photon-electron transfer matrix (transfer matrix operator) is T_{\gamma e} = T_{pp}:

  T_{\gamma e}(q) = 
  \begin{pmatrix}
    q - q^{-1} & 1 \\
    1 & 0
  \end{pmatrix}

Its characteristic polynomial is:

  \det(T_{\gamma e} - \lambda \mathbb{I})
  = 
  \lambda^2 - (q - q^{-1})\lambda - 1
  =  0

This yields the eigenvalues:

  \lambda_{\pm}(q)
  = 
  \frac{(q - q^{-1}) \pm \sqrt{(q - q^{-1})^2 + 4}}{2}

The discriminant is a perfect square, (q-q^{-1})^2 + 4 = q^2 + 2 + q^{-2} = (q+q^{-1})^2, so \sqrt{h^2+4} = [2]_q, the Temperley–Lieb loop parameter, and the eigenvalues are exact:

  \lambda_\pm = \frac{h \pm [2]_q}{2}
  = \frac{(q-q^{-1}) \pm (q+q^{-1})}{2},
  \qquad
  \lambda_+ = q, \qquad \lambda_- = -q^{-1}.

These are the Hecke generator's eigenvalues: \lambda^2 = h\lambda + 1, i.e. (\lambda-q)(\lambda+q^{-1}) = 0, which identifies this operator as \sigma_i.

At the aether parameter q_0:

  q - q^{-1} \approx 0.2091, \quad
  [2]_q \approx 2.010897, \quad
  \lambda_+ \approx 1.109979, \quad
  \lambda_- \approx -0.900918 .

Shell n from the n-th power

Shell n of an atom is the n-th power of the transfer matrix at the electron-nucleus junction. Each power corresponds to one R-I move (Reidemeister I). This adds one curl to the diagram of the electron's closure, increasing the writhe by 1 without altering the link type. (In the backup model the closure is the trefoil; under the electron ruling (electron) it is the Hopf link.)

Diagonalize T_{\gamma e} = S \Lambda S^{-1}:

  T_{\gamma e}^n
  = 
  S
  \begin{pmatrix}
    \lambda_+^n & 0 \\
    0 & \lambda_-^n
  \end{pmatrix}
  S^{-1}

The eigenvector matrix is:

  S = 
  \begin{pmatrix}
    \lambda_+ & \lambda_- \\
    1 & 1
  \end{pmatrix}

The entries of T_{\gamma e}^n are:

  (T^n)_{11}
  = 
  \frac{\lambda_+^{n+1} - \lambda_-^{n+1}}{\lambda_+ - \lambda_-},
  \qquad
  (T^n)_{21}
  = 
  \frac{\lambda_+^n - \lambda_-^n}{\lambda_+ - \lambda_-}

These correspond to Chebyshev polynomials of the second kind in the variable \frac{1}{2}(q - q^{-1}):

  (T^n)_{21} =  U_{n-1}\!\left(\tfrac{q - q^{-1}}{2}\right)

The traced volume at shell n

The Markov-traced volume at shell n is:

  \hat{V}(n, q)
  = 
  z \cdot (T^n)_{11} + (T^n)_{21}
  = 
  \frac{(z\lambda_+ + 1)\lambda_+^n - (z\lambda_- + 1)\lambda_-^n}
       {\lambda_+ - \lambda_-}

where z = q^{3}/(q^{2}+1) is the Markov parameter.

Define:

  \alpha =  z\lambda_+ + 1, \qquad
  \beta =  z\lambda_- + 1

This gives:

  \hat{V}(n, q) = 
  \frac{\alpha \cdot \lambda_+^n - \beta \cdot \lambda_-^n}
       {\lambda_+ - \lambda_-}

Since |\lambda_+| > 1 > |\lambda_-|, the dominant term for large n becomes:

  \hat{V}(n, q)  \sim 
  \frac{\alpha}{\lambda_+ - \lambda_-} \cdot \lambda_+^n
  \qquad (n \gg 1)

The sub-dominant term \beta \cdot \lambda_-^n = \beta \cdot (-1)^n / \lambda_+^n provides an alternating correction that decays exponentially.

The Chebyshev recurrence

The traced volumes satisfy the three-term recurrence:

  \boxed{
    \hat{V}(n+1, q)
    = 
    (q - q^{-1}) \cdot \hat{V}(n, q)
    + 
    \hat{V}(n-1, q)
  }

The initial conditions are \hat{V}(0, q) = 1 (no crossings) and \hat{V}(1, q) = z(q - q^{-1}) + 1 (one crossing).

The energy of shell n in hydrogen is:

  E_n(q)
  = 
  E_0 \cdot \hat{V}(n, q)

where E_0 sets the ground-state energy scale. This originates from the electron-proton crossing energy at the aether parameter q.

The transition energy (photon energy for n \to n+1) is:

  \Delta E_{n \to n+1}
  = 
  E_0 \bigl[\hat{V}(n+1, q) - \hat{V}(n, q)\bigr]
  = 
  E_0 \bigl[(q - q^{-1} - 1) \hat{V}(n, q)
  + \hat{V}(n-1, q)\bigr]

For the dominant term (n \gg 1):

  \Delta E_{n \to n+1}
   \sim 
  E_0 \cdot \frac{\alpha}{\lambda_+ - \lambda_-}
  \cdot \lambda_+^n \cdot (\lambda_+ - 1)

The Rydberg scaling E_n \propto 1/n^2 emerges in the regime \lambda_+ \approx 1 + \epsilon with \epsilon = \lambda_+ - 1 \ll 1. At the aether parameter q, \epsilon = 0.1073. For low shells (n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots):

  \lambda_+^n \approx e^{n\epsilon}
  \approx 1 + n\epsilon + \tfrac{1}{2}n^2\epsilon^2 + \cdots

The binding energy at shell n (relative to ionization) is:

  \mathfrak{E}_{\mathrm{bind}}(n)
  = 
  E_{\infty} - E_n
   \propto 
  \frac{1}{\lambda_+^n}
   \approx 
  e^{-n\epsilon}

For small \epsilon, this approximates 1/n^2 over the relevant range (n = 1 to \sim 7). The exact formula is the exponential \lambda_+^{-n}. This reproduces the Rydberg formula to the precision of low-n hydrogen spectroscopy.

Sub-shell structure from multi-electron tensor products

For atoms with Z electrons, the transfer matrix at each electron-nucleus generator is a tensor product:

  T_{\mathrm{total}}^{(i)}

The eigenvalues of the tensor product are products of individual eigenvalues: \lambda_{\pm}^{(1)} \cdot \lambda_{\pm}^{(2)} \cdots. The degeneracy structure of these products determines the sub-shells:

  • s orbital (\ell = 0): Both electrons occupy the same eigenstate \lambda_+^n (no angular node). Capacity: 2 (spin up/down).
  • p orbital (\ell = 1): One electron occupies \lambda_+, one occupies \lambda_- (one angular node from the alternating eigenvalue). Capacity: 6 (m = -1, 0, +1 times spin).
  • d orbital (\ell = 2): Two alternating eigenvalues (two angular nodes). Capacity: 10.

The angular momentum quantum number \ell counts how many electrons at shell n occupy the sub-dominant eigenvalue \lambda_-. The magnetic quantum number m projects the eigenvalue pattern onto the Reeb axis.

The capacity per sub-shell is 2(2\ell + 1). The capacity per shell is \sum_{\ell=0}^{n-1} 2(2\ell+1) = 2n^2.

  1. Start with \mathcal{N}(1, 0) = \mathbf{1} (identity in H_1(q)).
  2. Hopf-link the next nucleon: append crossings \sigma_j^{\epsilon(j,k)} for all existing nucleons j < k.
  3. Reduce via the Gröbner--Shirshov basis G = \{\sigma_i^2 - (q - q^{-1})\sigma_i - 1, \text{YB}, \text{far-comm}\}.
  4. Record the Hecke reduction energy \Delta E_k (Gröbner–Shirshov energy) and the word-length histogram h_k(\ell) = \#\{w \in \mathrm{supp}(\mathcal{N}) : |w| = \ell\}.

Repeat until A = p + n nucleons are linked.

Raw normal form (part (i))

\mathcal{N}(p, n) is in Gröbner--Shirshov normal form for every A \geq 1, by induction on A:

  • Base case. \mathcal{N}(1, 0) = \mathbf{1} is by definition in normal form (the empty word has no squares, no YB triples, no far-comm pairs).

  • Inductive step. Given \mathcal{N} at step A in normal form in H_A(q), the Hopf-link step produces

   \xi_{A+1}
   = 
   \mathcal{N}(A)
    \cdot 
   \prod_{j=0}^{A-1}(c_j \sigma_j + d_j)

where each factor (c_j \sigma_j + d_j) is the crossing element for the new nucleon with nucleon j (already in normal form: linear in \sigma_j, no squares). The product \xi_{A+1} may contain \sigma_j^2 terms from multiplying \sigma_j factors. Apply the Gröbner--Shirshov division algorithm (division algorithm) with the Hecke basis G:

   \mathcal{N}(A+1)
    := 
   r(\xi_{A+1}, G).

By the main theorem of Gröbner--Shirshov basis theory (main theorem):

  1. The algorithm terminates (the length-lex ordering on positive braid monomials is well-founded).
  2. The remainder r(\xi_{A+1}, G) is unique (independent of reduction path).
  3. The remainder is in normal form (no word in its support contains a leading monomial of any g \in G).

Therefore \mathcal{N}(A+1) is in normal form. \square

The normal form has at most A! terms (the dimension of H_A(q) over \mathbb{Z}[q^{\pm 1}], equal to |S_A|), a finite representation for any nucleus.

Optimal normal form

Proof sketch. The proof is by induction on A. Adding strand A creates cross-terms \sigma_i \cdot \sigma_{A-1} for all i < A - 1. Absorb these terms as follows:

  • If |i - (A-1)| \geq 2: Far-commutativity gives \sigma_{A-1} \cdot \sigma_i. Then I_{9} absorbs this term since the prefix \sigma_i is present.
  • If |i - (A-1)| = 1: This forms an adjacency pair. I_{8} absorbs this term since the prefix \sigma_{A-1} is present.
  • If i = A - 1: The Hecke relation yields \sigma_{A-1}^2 = (q - q^{-1})\sigma_{A-1} + \mathbf{1}. Both terms are already in the basis.

The identity term \mathbf{1} survives because d \neq 0 for nn and pn crossings. The condition N \geq Z - 1 ensures at least one nn or pn crossing exists at every generator. \square

This is verified computationally for all A \leq 8 (reducing 14,256 terms to 8 for {}^8\mathrm{Be}).

Valley of stability boundary. The optimality fails for N < Z - 1 (proton-heavy nuclei). When all crossings are pp type (d = 0), the identity term vanishes. Multiplying by (c \cdot \sigma_k + 0) does not preserve the identity. Without \mathbf{1} in the support, I_{9} chain-stripping lacks a root.

See Table 4.

The boundary N \geq Z - 1 matches the nuclear valley of stability.
def:gs-quotient-ideals-I8-I9:
Definition Quotient ideals I_8 (adjacency correlation) and I_9 (closed-shell chain collapse). The quotient ideals I_8 and I_9 act on the Gröbner--Shirshov normal form (shell closure normal form) as follows:

  • I_{8} (adjacency correlation): a reduced word \sigma_i \sigma_{i+1} of length 2 is absorbed into \sigma_{i+1} when the latter is present in the normal form.
  • I_{9} (closed shell chain collapse): a reduced word w \cdot \sigma_j is absorbed when its prefix w is present in the normal form.
rem:gs-quotient-ideals-i8-i9-remark: Remark Why the quotient ideals I_8 and I_9 reduce the normal form. The raw Gröbner--Shirshov normal form (shell closure normal form) contains up to A! terms. The quotient ideals I_8 and I_9 reduce this complexity by absorbing structurally-determined reduced words into the per-generator transfer-matrix factorisation. Under I_8, the coefficient of \sigma_i \sigma_{i+1} is structurally determined by the off-diagonal entry of the transfer matrix product M_i, rather than being independent. Under I_9, the absorption implements the per-generator transfer matrix factorization by replacing the expanded Hecke element with the product of \hat{V}_i volumes.
thm:optimal-normal-form-valley:
Theorem Optimal Gröbner–Shirshov normal form has exactly A terms in the valley of stability. The raw normal form contains up to A! terms. Quotienting by the adjacency and chain-collapse ideals reduces this to exactly A terms—the optimal Gröbner--Shirshov basis—for nuclei in the valley of stability (N \geq Z - 1).

Theorem (Optimal Normal Form). For any nucleus N(Z, N) with N \geq Z - 1 (valley of stability), the Gröbner--Shirshov normal form after applying quotient ideals I_{8} and I_{9} possesses exactly A = Z + N terms:

  \mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{opt}}(Z, N)
  = 
  c_0 \cdot \mathbf{1}
  + c_1 \cdot \sigma_0
  + c_2 \cdot \sigma_1
  + \cdots
  + c_{A-1} \cdot \sigma_{A-2}.

Each coefficient c_i = \hat{V}_i(q) is the Markov-traced volume derived from the transfer matrix chain at generator \sigma_i.

Remark Bruhat-symmetric shell filling and the shell-closure permutations. The Gröbner--Shirshov normal form \mathcal{N}(p, n) of a nucleus built by sequential Hopf linking (nuclear Gröbner--Shirshov reduction) exhibits a shell closure signature for doubly-magic configurations.

The Poincaré palindrome at (p, p) nuclei forces the Gröbner--Shirshov normal form to fill the entire Bruhat lattice of S_{2p} symmetrically. Every reduced word of length \ell pairs with a reduced word of length L - \ell having matching coefficient magnitude. This forms the algebraic signature of complete shell filling. All available crossing configurations within the shell are occupied. The structure is invariant under the Bruhat duality w \mapsto w_0 w, where w_0 is the longest element of S_{2p}.

The dominant word encodes the Borromean closure (the 3-body linking creating the shell). At each shell closure, the dominant word jumps to a significantly longer reduced word. Length 1 at A = 3 jumps to length 4 at A = 4, and length 9 at A = 7 jumps to length 16 at A = 8. This reflects the intertwining of all nucleons within the closed shell.

The dominant words at shell closures are specific reduced words in S_{2p}. These shell closure permutations maximally intertwine the p protons and p neutrons within the shell.

def:chebyshev-torus-coefficients:
Definition Chebyshev crossing coefficients of T_{2,n}. The torus knot T_{2,n} is the closure of \sigma^n in H_2(q). Its crossing coefficients (c_n, d_n) in the 2 \times 2 transfer matrix satisfy the Chebyshev recurrence:

  \boxed{
    c_n = U_{n-1}(\tfrac{q - q^{-1}}{2}),
    \qquad
    d_n = -\frac{c_n \cdot qs_q}{1 + c_n}
  }

where U_k is the Chebyshev polynomial of the second kind and s_q = q^{1/2} - q^{-1/2}.

Equivalently, from the matrix power T(1,0)^n = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix} a_n & c_n \\ c_n & d_n \end{smallmatrix}\bigr):

  c_1 = 1, \quad d_1 = 0
  \qquad\text{(bare crossing)}
  c_{n+1} = c_n(q - q^{-1}) + c_n + d_n, \qquad
  d_{n+1} = c_n

def:inter-shell-operator:
Definition Inter-shell torus-knot operator \Phi_{\mathrm{shell}}^{(\ell)}. Let shell \ell contain n_s nucleons and be closed. The inter-shell operator of shell \ell is

  \Phi_{\mathrm{shell}}^{(\ell)} \colon H_A(q) \to H_{A+1}(q),
  \qquad
  \bar{\mathcal{N}}_A \mapsto r\!\bigl(\bar{\mathcal{N}}_A \cdot (c_{n_s}\sigma + d_{n_s}), G\bigr),

where (c_{n_s}, d_{n_s}) are the Chebyshev crossing coefficients of T_{2, n_s}, and r(\cdot, G) denotes the Gröbner--Shirshov division algorithm.
rem:inter-shell-operator-remark: Remark Reading of the inter-shell operator. Closure of a shell is indicated by a palindromic histogram. The inter-shell operator is the torus-knot transfer matrix of T_{2,n_s}; it encodes the crossing of a new nucleon, which starts shell \ell + 1, with the closed shell \ell.
prop:torus-knot-shell-binding:
Proposition Withdrawn: shell binding from the torus knot hierarchy: T_{2,3} \to T_{2,5} \to T_{2,7} \to T_{2,9}. Withdrawn. The shell-size rule used here, that a closing shell of size n_s is bound by the torus knot T_{2,n_s}, is withdrawn. Its basis was a mislabel: (\sigma_0\sigma_1)^2\sigma_0 closes to T(2,4), not to the cinquefoil T(2,5). The rule stays withdrawn until it is derived. This block is kept as a record of the proposal, because other blocks cite it, and it is not a result.

Let q > 1, and build the nucleus by inductive Gröbner--Shirshov reduction, each shell-boundary crossing mediated by the inter-shell torus-knot operator \Phi_{\mathrm{shell}}^{(\ell)} (Chebyshev crossing coefficients of T_{2, n_s}). A shell closes exactly when the word-length histogram of \bar{\mathcal{N}}(p, n) is palindromic, at nucleon count A_{\mathrm{close}}, and the closing shell of size n_s = A_{\mathrm{close}} - A_{\mathrm{prev}} is bound by T_{2, n_s}. Each embeddable torus knot T_{r,s} on the Bring surface assigns a shell capacity

  \bigl|\mathrm{shell}(T_{r,s})\bigr| = r \times s

(see Table 2). The construction is proposed to reproduce the experimental magic numbers

  \{2,\, 8,\, 20,\, 28,\, 50,\, 82,\, 126\}

as cumulative same-type shell occupancies (see Table 3). Closing the full sequence as a from-q derivation — in particular reconciling the r\times s shell capacities with the Table-3 occupancies — is the key open problem, not established here. The Hecke energy gap at a shell boundary scales as |\lambda_+(T_{2,n_s})/\lambda_-(T_{2,n_s})| = q^{2 n_s}; for the first shell closure (He-4 \to Li-5),

  \frac{\Delta E_5}{\Delta E_4} \approx \frac{1.409}{0.095} = 14.8 .
